thread.title: Daseke: Expect Share Price Recovery On Improved Pricing, Execution And Sentiment - Daseke, Inc. (NASDAQ:DSKE)

author: Dane Capital Management, LLC
title: Daseke: Expect Share Price Recovery On Improved Pricing, Execution And Sentiment - Daseke, Inc. (NASDAQ:DSKE)
text:
Like several of our core holdings, Daseke ( DSKE ) got off to a rough start in 2018. It had a poorly executed follow-on offering in February that resulted in a 20%+ decline in share price during the roadshow, followed by a tepid 4Q report and the poorly received acquisition of Aveda, which was above historic acquisition multiples. We suspect that in a couple of quarters, investors will have a far more sanguine view about Aveda, given what should be enormous earnings growth in 2018. In addition, we believe the acquisition provides meaningful potential synergies and strategic benefits to Daseke.
We are confident Daseke will upwardly revise guidance following 2Q results. We expect improved pricing, increased fleet utilization, and better execution to drive shares higher and change investor sentiment. We note that a modest 1 1/2 turn expansion in Daseke's EV/EBITDA multiple would result in almost a $4 per share (40%) gain in stock price. Daseke has previously traded above this multiple.
Notwithstanding the issues earlier in the year, we believe things are likely to get much better from here for the company and for shareholders. For those unfamiliar with the Daseke story, the company filed an updated investor presentation on Monday or you could read our original top idea from March 2017.
Spot pricing for the flat-bed segment (39% of revenues) has been on fire this year, with prices up 31% y/y in May 2018 vs. May 2017. Daseke has 95% of its business on contract, but as contracts gradually come up for renewal, we anticipate prices to continue to rise for the company. In 1Q, rates per mile were up 6% y/y. We expect further expansion in 2Q. Specialized pricing was flat y/y in 1Q, but utilization improved, resulting in a 10.3% y/y increase in revenue per tractor. We suspect pricing will move higher in 2Q, and even more so in 2H. We also anticipate utilization to continue to improve. For example, management has been discussing the wind sector coming on exceptionally strongly in 2H. Notably, Vestas ( OTCPK:VWDRY ), the world's largest wind turbine manufacturer, is Daseke's 8th largest customer. Infrastructure and Energy Alternatives (IEA), a public renewables EPC largely focused on wind (see separate article out today ) has guided full year revenue that implies 3Q revenue 6x the level of 1Q. Even if Vestas is just 1.5% or 2.0% of revenue, if it grows anywhere in that ballpark, it would account for substantial growth for Daseke.
We're not aware of anyone among Daseke's top 10 customers (28% of revenue) that doesn't expect continued growth in the back half of 2018. Source: Daseke June Investor Presentation , page 13
We think higher pricing and higher utilization are a recipe for substantial growth and margin expansion.
Currently, the Street is modeling 2019 EBITDA of $164 million. Given the company has $159 million of trailing 12-month EBITDA through the end of March, we believe there will be a sizable upward revision when the company reports 2Q results, likely towards the $175-180 million range. We also think that greater efficiency from the 7 acquisitions the company made in 2017 should generate greater benefits in coming quarters and 2019.
Source: Daseke June Investor Presentation , page 16
In addition to the bar being set low in terms of expectations and valuation, Daseke is in the enviable position of being in an industry anticipated to experience accelerating growth in coming years. We don't recall having previously seen the below slide, but it certainly bodes well and is consistent with spot price and load-to-truck trends.
Source: Daseke June Investor Presentation , page 11
Since becoming public, one of the criticisms of Daseke has been that they've shown modest organic growth (we expect that to change) and have not exhibited operational excellence. On May 14th, Daseke established Daseke Fleet Services ("DFS") and announced the hiring of three long-tenured Swift Transportation - now Knight-Swift Transportation ( KNX ) - supply chain executives: Brett Thompson as vice president of purchasing, Erek Starnes as vice president of equipment operations, and Gloria Pliler as director of purchasing. Their mandate is to leverage purchasing, equipment optimization, and maintenance.
Source: Daseke June Investor Presentation , page 27
Following the press release, we spoke to Daseke President Scott Wheeler to get a better understanding of the rationale for the establishment of DFS, given management has previously suggested that they already enjoy scale benefits (i.e. lower fuel costs, elimination of redundant insurance coverage). Mr. Wheeler indicated that he thought Daseke was enjoying scale benefits, and they were doing a good job, but they could be great. He summed by stating that at the company's current size, "if DFS adds 100bps to margins, and we're continuing to grow, we're talking real money." By our estimates, if they can achieve a 100bps improvement by 2020, that's an additional $20 million, with virtually all of that falling to the bottom line.
We understand that much of investing is driven by sentiment. In a prior article , we wrote about the importance of patience in investing and commented on several companies. In the article, we discussed XPO Logistics ( XPO ), now a $12-billion market cap logistics player, as an analog to Daseke (in part because they share a common roll-up strategy). From June 2015 to January 2016, which was not a bad time for the trucking/transportation sector, the stock declined 64%. Since XPO hit its lows, the stock is more than a 5-bagger in 2 1/2 years (it hit $18.06 on January 20, 2016).
We don't think Daseke is particularly different than the $14+ per share company it was in January. If anything, the company is probably wiser based on the things that went wrong in the 1st half, and particularly well-positioned to benefit from strengthening in the 2nd half and beyond.
However, sentiment has clearly changed. In one of the more absurd things we've heard lately, a sell-side analyst told us that a number of institutions won't touch the stock because Don Daseke and other insiders will receive 5 million shares this year if the stock is above $14 for 20 of 30 trading days and they achieve $170 million in EBITDA. These investors are suggesting that Daseke do the "right thing" and walk away from the potential shares. We think this is ridiculous. To be clear:
Daseke can't recklessly make acquisitions to increase EBITDA, but actually needs to see the stock appreciate to receive earn-out shares, creating value for himself and investors alike. With over 30% ownership and a lock-up until March 2020, Mr. Daseke is exceptionally aligned. This wasn't recently added to Don Daseke's pay package but was a condition negotiated in the original SPAC merger with Hennessy Capital Acquisition Corp. 2 - a condition without which, the merger likely wouldn't have occurred. All the shares don't go to Mr. Daseke, but go to a number of executives, so it's not really his choice anyway. This didn't seem to weigh on investors in January when the stock was at $14. This strikes us as a lot of nonsense, and some investors trying to justify their malaise by creating a false narrative.
After all, a stock can appreciate after a CEO is granted an absolutely ridiculous pay package. We need look no further than Tesla ( TSLA ) and Elon Musk. Proxy advisers ISS and Glass Lewis denounced Musk's new pay package.
Many may question the reasonableness of billions of dollars in pay opportunity, no matter how demanding the performance requirements. Even when annualized, Musk's pay opportunity would dwarf that of nearly every CEO at the largest and most profitable public companies.
Institutional Shareholder Services report
A view also shared by many academics.
This is a guy who's promising to send people to Mars. He thinks big. It's worked for him. He's a billionaire. But I do question why he needs it to begin with. It's not like he's using it to motivate his employees or other managers.
Steven Balsam, compensation specialist and professor at Temple University's Fox School of Business.
As well as from forensic accountants.
Despite the possibility that he could get zilch, the pay package doesn't focus on the right things. There's a lack of emphasis on profits and production. The new plan stands in contrast to the previous scheme, which required Musk to hit production, gross margin, and new model targets.
David Trainer, CEO of New Constructs , Forensic Accounting Specialist
Despite Musk's generous pay package, Tesla's shares are up 8% since it was approved by shareholders on March 21st and had been up more than 20% until the stock's recent decline.
This is not to suggest that Elon Musk isn't a visionary. We personally have a strong preference for the pay packages of Steve Jobs who earned a base salary of just $1 per year from 1997 to 2011 while serving as CEO of Apple ( AAPL ) and Warren Buffett, CEO of Berkshire Hathaway ( BRK.A ) who took home just $100,000 in salary last year - with both men realizing additional wealth would be created through stock price appreciation. Our point is that ludicrous pay packages don't stop stocks from going up if sentiment is favorable. If Tesla was at a 52-week low, we're confident investor feedback would have been quite different.
Don Daseke did not request his earn-out shares to be re-struck with lower price requirement because his stock dropped. His package was negotiated and in the public domain since December 2016. Conversely, Musk, who has more money than one could ever reasonably spend, just received a pile more, without investors abandoning his stock.
That sophisticated investors would use Daseke's package (which is not simply pay, but part of the price for which he sold his company) as a reason to avoid the stock indicates how brutal sentiment currently is. However, we view this as an opportunity. A shift in sentiment, driven by better execution and results could drive a dramatic uplift in shares.
We believe there is a lot of open road ahead for Daseke, and they continue to be exceptionally positioned to consolidate a highly fragmented industry. We are optimistic that results will improve significantly in coming quarters as will the company's share price. We are confident that we will be rewarded for our patience and believe that with a free cash flow yield that should exceed 10% in 2019 (possibly approaching the low teens) assuming normalized 5-7% capex, there is limited downside to shares at current prices.
